newsitem.title: CHINA: Long March 3B carries China's space industry flag.
newsitem.headline: Long March 3B carries China's space industry flag.

text.p: When China next lights the fire under a new-generation Long March 3B rocket, far more will be at stake than just the multimillion-dollar satellite on board.

Analysts say success would go a long way towards restoring confidence in China's space industry and erasing the memory of the maiden flight of a 3B in February 1996, when the rocket veered off course and exploded, killing at least six people.

More than a year after that disaster and after a series of successful domestic launches, Beijing was now ready to bring back the Long March 3B to fire two international satellites aloft, said Zhang Lihui of state launcher China Aerospace Industry Co.

China Aerospace would launch the Philippines communications satellite Mabuhay and the Apstar 2R orbiter owned by the Beijing-controlled Hong Kong firm APT Satellite Holdings Ltd, Zhang said in a telephone interview.
"We will use the Long March 3B for the two satellites," she said. "The first flight of a Long March 3B was a failure, but after a year's effort, its problems have been resolved."
The three-stage, liquid-fuelled 3B, which can fire 4.8-tonne satellites into orbit with the help of four strap-on boosters, is seen as a powerful addition to the Long March rocket family.
China has been hungry for satellite success since its launch industry -- long admired for its low costs and high reliability -- stumbled into a series of disasters in early 1995.
In January that year, a Long March 2E rocket carrying the original Apstar 2 satellite blew up shortly after blast-off, killing a family of six in a rain of fiery debris.

Then came the February 1996 loss of the first 3B and its U.S.-built Intelsat 708 satellite payload, followed in August by the failure of a Long March 3 rocket to put its Chinasat-7 orbiter into the proper orbit.
The setbacks, while hardly uncommon in the high-risk satellite business, put China's launch industry on the line by forcing up already hefty insurance premiums paid by customers.
China's technicians had been working hard to review quality standards and cut the risk of any mishap marring the Apstar 2R and Mabuhay launches, said one Beijing-based industry analyst.
"I think they have overcome their problems and they've learnt from the lessons of the past," said the analyst. "I don't think there will be a major problem."
Beijing's two domestic come-back launches this year, of a weather satellite aboard a Long March 3 and a communications orbiter on a 3A, had boosted international confidence, he said.
An official with China's Launch Vehicle Institute said the fault that caused the 1996 3B loss -- an electrical problem in the direction-controlling inertial platform -- had been fixed.
"We have resolved the problem now, and the same platform was used in the recent successful launch of the Long March 3A," the official said.
Prospects seemed good for a pair of successful launches that would put China back on its space track, said Peter Jackson, chief executive of Hong Kong-based satellite company Asiasat.

"As long as there is no fundamental design flaw in the 3B, then I would think they will be very successful," Jackson said. "If you see two good launches, Mabuhay and Apstar 2R, I think that's going to put the Chinese into a very strong position."
Despite the higher premiums caused by the string of failures, insurance for Apstar 2R had been placed very successfully, said a Beijing-based insurance source.
Apstar 2R had given China an opportunity to show its confidence in placing international reinsurance, the source said, adding that past losses meant tensions remained high.
"Everybody is very nervous and very anxious about this launch," he said.
